name: Aaron Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a neighbourhood supermarket on a big new housing estate, the only proper shop for about two miles. I'm on the tills in the morning and on goods-in in the afternoon, checking the lorry, scanning pallets and filling the chillers. I like goods-in more, because you see how the whole shop actually works. What wears me out is customers who want to argue about a coupon at eight in the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what's your situation outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eight years, and I'm on the higher rate because I'm trusted with deliveries and the ordering gun. I live with my girlfriend Selin, who works in her family's restaurant. I've got about seven months of pay in cash and another chunk in shares, mostly retail and tech firms. I use AI every day, for reading company reports, planning my budget and checking deliveries against invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market sorted it out, like it always does. Online I'd post that the hype was overpriced and the shares fell back to earth. At work I'd say the same thing, but simpler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. My job's safe, and my shares would just track the economy. I'd keep doing what I do and keep investing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep putting three hundred a month into shares. I'd ask about the assistant manager role in a year or two. I might look at opening a little shop on the next estate one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Business as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your own shop? Say more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a new estate going up across the bypass with no shop at all. A small shop with self-checkouts and one person on the floor could work on the new estate. It's a dream for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any pressure even in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selin's family restaurant has thin margins, and her dad wants her to take it over. That's a big decision for us. AI doesn't change that.

I'd post that AI was **overpriced** and the shares fell back to earth.
think: My **job's safe** and my shares would just track the economy.
I'd keep doing what I do and keep **investing**.
do: Keep my job and put **£300 a month** into shares.
Ask about the **assistant manager** role in a year or two.
S0.quote: A small shop with self-checkouts and one person on the floor could work on the new estate.
fieldNote: He thinks like an **owner**, dreaming of his own small shop.
His real pressure is **Selin's family restaurant** and whether she takes it over.
He uses AI daily and holds **shares**, unusual for a cashier.

steps.text: Keep the morning tills and afternoon goods-in shifts
Put 300 a month into retail and tech shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, and people who work hard and learn will be fine. I'd post about it positively. At work I'd tell colleagues to try the new ordering tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The ordering on the gun would go to software, which I already half use. Robots come slowly, so I'd have time to move toward owning something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new ordering system first and offer to train others. I'd put more into shares in the firms making robots. I'd start saving a separate fund for my own shop, about two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work might struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our cleaner Barry, who's sixty and doesn't have a smartphone. He's a good man. I'd hope the company finds him something, but it's not the government's job to keep him in work forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you automate your own shop if you had one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, of course, that's the point. I'd automate my own shop with self-checkouts and AI ordering, but I'd still want a person greeting people.

fieldNote: He welcomes **automation** as a future shop owner.

He separates a **shop fund** from his share portfolio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt fast, and don't wait for the government. I'd post about owning a piece of the change through shares or a business. At work I'd be blunt: start planning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my supermarket job goes by 2031, both the tills and goods-in. The 2028 part takes the ordering straight away. My shares would probably do well, but I don't know if that covers a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open the small shop on the new estate within a year, using my shop fund and some shares. I'd automate it from day one. I'd keep a few months of cash untouched in case it fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more busy than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Doesn't a robot shop face the same threat as your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a way, yes. But I'd own the robots instead of being replaced by them. If big chains move in, I'd sell up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Selin say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say do it, but don't bet the house. Her family's restaurant would face the same thing. We'd plan both together at the kitchen table.

fieldNote: He answers fast AGI by becoming an **owner**, not a worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good run-up, so get going. I'd post about it, mostly positive. At work I'd encourage people to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have until 2031 for the ordering and 2034 for the floor work. That's time to open my shop and grow it. I'm fairly relaxed about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job for two years while I plan the shop. Then I'd open it, automated, on the new estate. I'd keep investing a bit each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, mostly confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone else has the same idea. If everyone has the same idea, there'll be robot shops on every corner and margins go to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you help family with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd help Selin's dad automate the restaurant ordering. Family business first. That's how we'd both get through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone with ambition. I'd post about starting businesses. At work I'd tell people to pick something and go for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one's easy for me. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come, with my own shop or two, buying robots instead of fearing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for assistant manager first, learn the business side. Then I'd open my shop around thirty. I'd keep investing and maybe buy a small building for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any risks you can see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that I get comfortable and don't act. Ten years can slip by. I'd set myself deadlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you marry Selin in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably in the next couple of years. Family's important to me. I'd want that settled before the shop.

fieldNote: A decade lets him build **management skills** before owning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to build the shop properly, and Selin's family would be hit too. What would help is low taxes and easy rules for small businesses. Maybe cheap loans for people who want to start one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about ownership. Some of us want to own the change, not just survive it. That's how I think about it.

headlineQuote: Some of us want to own the change, not just survive it.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old** cashier and goods-in worker at a neighbourhood supermarket, eight years in.
He has seven months of cash plus a **share portfolio**, and lives with Selin.
He uses **AI daily** and dreams of an automated shop of his own.
Faster AGI pushes him to open his **shop sooner**; slower AGI lets him build up first.
He favours **markets and family** over government help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to build his shop and Selin's family would suffer too.
whatWouldHelp: **Low taxes**, easy rules and cheap loans for people starting small businesses.
